nameStory: The "black" in black locust refers to its deeply furrowed, dark bark that becomes almost charcoal-colored on mature trees. "Locust" comes from the belief that these trees bore the edible pods that sustained John the Baptist in the wilderness - though that was likely a different plant entirely!
description: Black locust is a medium-sized deciduous tree that typically grows 40-60 feet tall with a narrow, upright crown. It's instantly recognizable in late spring when it erupts in drooping clusters of fragrant white flowers that smell like orange blossoms. The tree has compound leaves made up of small, oval leaflets and distinctive deeply grooved bark on older trunks. Despite being native to only small areas of the southeastern US, it has spread widely and is now common throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Drooping clusters of white, pea-like flowers in late May to early June that smell intensely sweet and fragrant - you can smell them from quite a distance on a warm day

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-19 small, smooth oval leaflets arranged in pairs along a central stem, feeling thin and papery to the touch

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature bark is deeply furrowed with thick, interlacing ridges that feel rough and corky, becoming very dark brown to nearly black

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, brown pods 2-4 inches long that hang in clusters and rattle when shaken, persisting through winter

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Often grows in dense colonies from root sprouts, creating groves of similarly-aged trees with straight, narrow trunks

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Young branches and trunk sprouts armed with paired thorns up to 1 inch long - handle with care!

habitat: Black locust thrives in disturbed areas like old fields, roadsides, forest edges, and abandoned lots throughout New England. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun, often forming dense stands on slopes and in areas with poor or rocky soil where other trees struggle. You'll frequently find it growing alongside other pioneer species like gray birch and red maple.

seasonality.spring: Compound leaves emerge late in spring, followed by the spectacular show of drooping white flower clusters in late May to early June that fill the air with sweet fragrance.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage of light green compound leaves provides dappled shade, while flat seed pods begin developing from the spent flowers.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn pale yellow before dropping early, often while other trees are still green, revealing the dark furrowed bark and persistent brown seed pods.
seasonality.winter: Easily identified by distinctive deeply grooved dark bark, rattling seed pods, and paired thorns on younger growth, plus the characteristic colony-forming growth pattern.

funFact: Black locust wood is so rot-resistant that fence posts made from it can last over 100 years in the ground - longer than treated lumber! Early colonists called it "the wood that lasts forever" and used it for everything from ship masts to railroad ties.
confusionNotes: The white flower clusters might remind you of elderberry, but elderberry flowers are flat-topped, not drooping, and elderberry lacks the thorns and compound leaves. Remember: locust droops and has thorns, elderberry is flat and thornless.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting an African connection (like acacia trees), black locust is actually native to North America. Early botanists called it "false acacia" because its flowers and pods reminded them of true acacias, but they're only distantly related within the legume family.
compareHints: Black locust differs from its relatives bristly locust and clammy locust mainly by size and texture - it's much larger (a full-sized tree vs. shrubs) and lacks the sticky or bristly hairs on stems and seed pods that give the other species their names. Black locust also has the distinctive paired thorns that are less prominent or absent in its smaller cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike black locust which grows into a tall tree with thorny branches, bristly locust stays shrub-sized and has soft bristles instead of hard thorns.
Among the locust trees, clammy locust stands out with its pink flowers and sticky twigs, while black locust has white flowers and smooth branches.
